## Common themes

- Example papers
- Course structure
- Policies and logistics

::: {.notes}
Thank students for the feedback. Explain that these slides address themes
that appeared across multiple responses, plus several questions for which a
short clarification may be useful to everyone.
:::

## Can we see past projects?

- **Verdict:** No
- **Why:** respect student privacy and avoid limiting creativity
- **Similar format:** [American Economic Review: Insights](https://www.aeaweb.org/journals/aeri), [Journal of Public Economics (Short Papers)](https://www.sciencedirect.com/journal/journal-of-public-economics), [Reveiw of Economics and Statistics (Short Papers)](https://direct.mit.edu/rest), and [Journal of Urban Economics: Insights](https://www.sciencedirect.com/journal/journal-of-urban-economics)

::: {.notes}
The bureaucratic reason is respect for student privacy. The more important
substantive reason is that past projects can become templates and limit the
range of ideas students consider.

The linked venues provide a rough sense of the content of a short economics
paper. Their articles are more developed and polished than the projects
expected in this course.
:::

## Can we read more economics papers?

- **Verdict:** Yes, in service of your project
- **Why:** build skill of efficient skimming and situate project in literature
- **Plan:** short reading guidance memo and an in-class exercise

::: {.notes}
The goal is to help students read papers efficiently while avoiding an early
focus on existing work that could narrow their search for ideas. The memo will
provide a practical reading strategy, which students will then use in class.
:::

## Can we have more lectures?

- **Verdict:** Keep the planned structure
- **Why:** more lectures come at the expense of fewer (universally liked!) 1-on-1 meetings or communication practice

::: {.notes}
Students strongly valued the individual meetings. One student requested more
lectures, but the course will continue to prioritize individualized feedback.
This choice also explains why the final exam remains in the final exam period.
:::

## Can the final exam count less or happen earlier?

- **Verdict:** No
- **Why:** exam disincentivizes cognitive offloading and pre-exam week timing crowds out meetings
- **Expectation:** nothing to study for if you have ownership over the project you submit

::: {.notes}
The exam checks that each student understands the work submitted during the
semester. Holding it during the final exam period preserves class time for
individual meetings and project preparation.
:::

## Can we collaborate more with peers?

- **Verdict:** Individual-meeting class sessions heavily involve group exercises and peer feedback
- **Boundary:** submitted assignments remain individual work

::: {.notes}
Students will collaborate while classmates rotate through individual meetings
with the instructor and TA. Keeping submitted assignments individual balances
the benefits of collaboration with ownership of each project.
:::

## Will final drafts use a scripted language?

- **Verdict:** Yes. Quarto rather than LaTeX
- **Why:** one-click reproducibility and publication-ready output
- **Sequence:** manual prose drafting first, migration at the end

::: {.notes}
The initial manual drafting constraint is pedagogical: students need to
practice writing and revising prose themselves. At the end of the course, they
will move the paper into Quarto so that text, results, and formatting can be
generated together. This is the workflow they should use in future research.
:::

## Will we cover research proposals?

- **Verdict:** Not as core course content
- **Why:** the format depends on the proposal's purpose
- **Support:** bring a specific proposal type to office hours

::: {.notes}
A grant proposal, an NSF proposal, and an internal research plan serve
different purposes. Students are welcome to ask for advice in office hours
once they know what kind of proposal they need to write.
:::

## Can the absence policy be more flexible?

- **Verdict:** The policy remains
- **Why:** absences reduce your learning and your classmates' feedback

::: {.notes}
The course depends on discussion, peer response, and individual feedback.
Attendance therefore affects both the absent student and the rest of the
class. The syllabus already explains the allowance for unexcused absences and
the process for excused absences.
:::

## Can assignments be posted on Canvas?

- **Verdict:** Yes. Done

::: {.notes}
This request has already been incorporated.
:::
